第2️⃣天：一整天深度玩转阿尔山秋景，早起看不动河的晨雾，河流边还有牛牛和漫山遍野的金黄橙红交织，午后光线柔和林间光影刚好，随手拍出森系治愈大片
·

·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·
第6️⃣天：上午欣赏额尔古纳草原初秋的湿地黄绿渐变河道蜿蜒，成群的牛马过水美的不像话，下午奔赴莫日格勒河俯瞰天下第一曲水壮阔又温柔，在落日余晖下我们疯狂拍照记录下开心时刻，返回海拉尔吃了心心念念的俄餐
第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程

items.text:
Anne Hathaway Goes Full ‘Jurassic Park’ in a Sci-Fi Hit Officially Taking Over Streaming

Image via Warner Bros. Pictures

Published Sep 21, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

The newly announced partner to Tom Cruise in Day of Thunder 2, Anne Hathaway, is currently having the busiest year of her career. Soon, she will debut her final big-screen installment of a huge 2026, as she reunites with director Michael Showalter — who previously directed her in Prime Video’s The Idea of You — in Verity, the latest in a flurry of Colleen Hoover adaptations on the big screen. Verity will also star the likes of Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett​​​​, and promises to be the darkest Hoover adaptation yet.

Verity is Hathaway's fifth and final film of a year in which she is also expecting her third child. This all began with her most underrated performance of 2026 in the criminally underseen Mother Mary. She then rejoined Meryl Streep, Stanley Tucci, and Emily Blunt for The Devil Wears Prada 2, which was called "a near-perfect blend of nostalgia and newness" by Collider's own Taylor Gates, before setting her sights on the film that might just come to define 2026: Christopher Nolan's historical epic The Odyssey.

As Penelope, Hathaway stole several scenes in The Odyssey, as she waited for Matt Damon's King of Ithaca to return whilst silently overseeing his kingdom. The film has outperformed even the highest expectations many had for it, being considered a lock for most of the major Academy Awards categories for next year and also grossing more than $1.7 billion worldwide, which marks a record for most involved. Following The Odyssey, and before tackling Verity, Hathaway dropped her most bonkers film of the year, one that has now become an instant hit on streaming.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Personality Quiz
Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like?
Paul Atreides · Captain Kirk · Princess Leia · Ellen Ripley · Max Rockatansky

Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🏜️Paul Atreides

🖖Capt. Kirk

✊Princess Leia

🔦Ellen Ripley

🔥Max Rockatansky

FIND YOUR HERO →

01

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?
The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you.

AI absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward.
BI read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes.
CI rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction.
DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.
EI don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?
The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails.

APrescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly.
BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.
CConviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire.
DComposure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury.
EEndurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for?
Your deepest motivation is your truest compass.

AThe survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it.
BThe safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind.
CFreedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire.
DThe truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not.
EThe one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you relate to the people around you?
Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

AWith intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated.
BWith warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself.
CWith directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it.
DWith professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family.
EWith wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do?
How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything.

APrepare in silence. If they won't listen, I'll be ready when they finally have to.
BKeep pushing until someone listens — and if no one does, handle it myself.
CBuild the case, find the allies, and make the threat impossible to ignore.
DDocument everything. The truth matters even if no one believes it yet.
EStop trying to convince anyone. Survive it. That's the only argument that counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

What has your heroism cost you personally?
Every hero pays. The question is what — and whether they'd pay it again.

AMy innocence — I've seen what I'm capable of, and I can't unsee it.
BPeople I loved — the command chair has a view, but it's a lonely one.
CA normal life — I gave up everything ordinary the moment I chose the cause.
DMy sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise.
EAlmost everything — and I'm still not sure what I'm carrying it all for. But I keep going.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

How do you feel about the rules of the world you're in?
Every hero has a relationship with the system. What's yours?

AI understand them deeply — and I know exactly which ones must be broken, and why.
BI respect the spirit of them and bend the letter when the situation demands it.
CThe system is the problem. I'm not here to work within it — I'm here to dismantle it.
DI follow protocol until protocol stops being useful. Then I make the call myself.
EThe rules collapsed a long time ago. What's left is instinct, and mine are reliable.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

When everything is on the line, what keeps you going?
The answer is the most honest thing about you.

ADestiny — or something that feels so much like it that the difference no longer matters.
BThe people on my ship — their faces, their trust, the fact that they're counting on me.
CThe belief that what we're fighting for is worth every sacrifice, including this one.
DSheer refusal to let it win — whatever it is. I don't stop. That's just who I am.
EI'm not sure anymore. But the road is still there, and I'm still on it.

REVEAL MY HERO →

Your Hero Has Been Identified
Your Sci-Fi Hero Is…

Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.

Arrakis · Dune

Paul Atreides

You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.

You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you.

You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape.

Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway.

That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you.

USS Enterprise · Star Trek

Captain Kirk

You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.

You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously.

Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it.

Kirk's genius isn't tactical — it's human. He reads people, bends rules with purpose, and wills outcomes into existence through sheer conviction.

That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours.

The Rebellion · Star Wars

Princess Leia

You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.

You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable.

You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back.

Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.

That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.

The Nostromo · Alien

Ellen Ripley

You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.

You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.

Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.

You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.

When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.

The Wasteland · Mad Max

Max Rockatansky

You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.

You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.

Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.

Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.

That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

In the Spielberg-esque sci-fi thriller The End of Oak Street, Hathaway joins Star Wars legend Ewan McGregor to fight a prehistoric threat as her quiet suburban life is inexplicably transported through time. The End of Oak Street ultimately disappointed during its theatrical run, earning just $120 million against a reported budget of $85 million. Thankfully, its recent move to streaming has already paid off, as The End of Oak Street currently ranks as the most-watched movie on the Apple TV store in the U.S.

Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one.
🏜️Paul Atreides
🖖Capt. Kirk
✊Princess Leia
🔦Ellen Ripley
🔥Max Rockatansky

FIND YOUR HERO →

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?
The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you.

AI absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward.
BI read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes.
CI rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction.
DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.
EI don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving.
NEXT QUESTION →

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?
The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails.

APrescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly.
BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.
CConviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire.
DComposure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury.
EEndurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped.
NEXT QUESTION →

What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for?
Your deepest motivation is your truest compass.

AThe survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it.
BThe safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind.
CFreedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire.
DThe truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not.
EThe one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for.
NEXT QUESTION →
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar53506159.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

How do you relate to the people around you?
Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

AWith intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated.
BWith warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself.
CWith directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it.
DWith professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family.
EWith wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds.
NEXT QUESTION →

You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do?
How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything.

APrepare in silence. If they won't listen, I'll be ready when they finally have to.
BKeep pushing until someone listens — and if no one does, handle it myself.
CBuild the case, find the allies, and make the threat impossible to ignore.
DDocument everything. The truth matters even if no one believes it yet.
EStop trying to convince anyone. Survive it. That's the only argument that counts.
NEXT QUESTION →

What has your heroism cost you personally?
Every hero pays. The question is what — and whether they'd pay it again.

AMy innocence — I've seen what I'm capable of, and I can't unsee it.
BPeople I loved — the command chair has a view, but it's a lonely one.
CA normal life — I gave up everything ordinary the moment I chose the cause.
DMy sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise.
EAlmost everything — and I'm still not sure what I'm carrying it all for. But I keep going.
NEXT QUESTION →

How do you feel about the rules of the world you're in?
Every hero has a relationship with the system. What's yours?
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar53563804-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

AI understand them deeply — and I know exactly which ones must be broken, and why.
BI respect the spirit of them and bend the letter when the situation demands it.
CThe system is the problem. I'm not here to work within it — I'm here to dismantle it.
DI follow protocol until protocol stops being useful. Then I make the call myself.
EThe rules collapsed a long time ago. What's left is instinct, and mine are reliable.
NEXT QUESTION →

When everything is on the line, what keeps you going?
The answer is the most honest thing about you.

ADestiny — or something that feels so much like it that the difference no longer matters.
BThe people on my ship — their faces, their trust, the fact that they're counting on me.
CThe belief that what we're fighting for is worth every sacrifice, including this one.
DSheer refusal to let it win — whatever it is. I don't stop. That's just who I am.
EI'm not sure anymore. But the road is still there, and I'm still on it.
REVEAL MY HERO →

Your Hero Has Been Identified
Your Sci-Fi Hero Is…
Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.
Arrakis · Dune
Paul Atreides
You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.
You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you.
You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/12/amazon01_logo-1.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway.
That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you.
USS Enterprise · Star Trek
Captain Kirk
You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.
You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously.
Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it.
Kirk's genius isn't tactical — it's human. He reads people, bends rules with purpose, and wills outcomes into existence through sheer conviction.
That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours.
The Rebellion · Star Wars
Princess Leia
You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.
You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable.
You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back.
Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.
That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.
The Nostromo · Alien
Ellen Ripley
You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.
You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.
Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.
You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.
When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.
The Wasteland · Mad Max
Max Rockatansky
You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.
You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.
Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.
Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.
That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

Published Sep 20, 2026, 11:57 PM EDT

Jessica is a young writer from Brisbane, Australia. An avid consumer and lover of all things Film and TV, you will never tear her away from a screen. A tendency rooted from childhood, she once had dreams of becoming a member of the famed kids-band 'Hi-5'. Perhaps that's what pushed her to secure an education with a theater background. But now, as dreams evolved, her passions have turned to admiring performances from afar. Frankly, she's just grateful that she can put her binging skills to good use. Outside of work, Jessica recently completed her undergraduate double degree in Arts/Communications. Other than that, she spends most of her free time with family and friends, probably never forgetting to talk about the new movie or show she watched the day prior.

HBO has never been particularly interested in making television that stays in one lane. After all, the network is responsible for prestige dramas, bleak thrillers, sprawling fantasies, and some of the most miserable families ever put on screen. However, it also knows how to make a show that's just an absolute hoot to watch. Sometimes that means rapid-fire comedy and outrageous situations, while other times it comes from spectacular action or a cast that's simply having the time of its life.

As such, these are the shows that bring something different to the table, whether it's a period drama, a vigilante tale, or a political comedy. At the end of the day, they're funny, energetic, wildly entertaining, and most importantly, the kind of shows that make it very easy to hit "next episode." So, if you find yourself sitting in a little funk, do yourself a favor and click on one of these.

8
'Warrior' (2019–2023)

Image Via HBO

Set in San Francisco's Chinatown in the late 19th century, Ah Sahm (Andrew Koji) is a martial arts prodigy who arrives from China in search for his missing sister. Unfortunately, his plans go devastatingly awry when he's suddenly sold to one of Chinatown's most powerful tongs, forcing him to navigate through a violent struggle for power in a town filled with rival gangs and corrupt politicians.

Combining brutal action with intense drama and a surprisingly playful sense of humor, it's no wonder that Warrior is a huge blast to watch. The fight scenes are, of course, a major draw, and yet the show's willingness to bounce between gang warfare, institutional corruption, and community dysfunction is what keeps it from becoming one-note. Plus, this show is based on an original concept by Bruce Lee himself—a fact that naturally brings an irreverent energy to the project's core.

7
'Peacemaker' (2022–2025)

Image via HBO Max

After surviving the events of The Suicide Squad, Chris Smith (John Cena)—better known as the brutal vigilante Peacemaker—is forced to join a black-ops team on the mysterious Project Butterfly. Here, he and his mismatched team of operatives must stop a mysterious alien invasion that soon becomes a threat far stranger than anything they expected.

In true James Gunn fashion, Peacemaker finds its magic by turning a ridiculous superhero into the center of a surprisingly heartfelt comedy—all without sanding away everything that makes him awful. Leaning into Peacemaker's macho posturing, bizarre musical tastes, and dysfunctional relationships is what helps create endless opportunities for comedy. It's also a plus that the rest of the team is a collection of equally entertaining foils. Just look at the vibrancy (and commitment) to the opening title dance sequence. That alone highlights the tone of this show.

6
'Our Flag Means Death' (2022–2023)

Image via HBO MAX

In the 18th century, wealthy aristocrat Stede Bonnet (Rhys Darby) grows tired of his privileged (and very cushy) life. As a result, he abandons everything and decides to become a pirate even though he has absolutely no idea what to do. But now, after assembling an equally unconventional crew for his ship, Stede must quickly figure things out, especially as he soon crosses paths with the legendary pirate Blackbeard (Taiki Waititi).

There's no doubt that the show's greatest strength is the sheer ridiculousness of its pirate world. Waititi's Blackbeard is less a fearsome pirate than a bored celebrity in need of a new direction, while Darby's Stede approaches piracy with the enthusiasm of someone organizing a particularly ill-advised dinner party. The result is a warm, absurd comedy where swashbuckling, disastrous schemes, and surprisingly sincere conversations about identity and love can all exist in the same episode. If only Our Flag Means Death didn't fall victim to the cancelation curse.

5
'Curb Your Enthusiasm' (2000–2024)

Image via HBO

As a fictionalized version of himself, Larry David is a successful television writer and producer whose life would probably be much easier if he simply stopped arguing with everyone. Instead, Larry has a remarkable talent for turning minor social annoyances into full-blown disasters, whether he's dealing with friends, family, celebrities, or complete strangers.

Frankly, there's no better fun than watching a person play an exaggerated version of themselves. And somehow David has managed to prolong that joke for over two decades—without running the humor dry. The loose improvisational style of Curb Your Enthusiasm has let audiences sit in the cringe of second-hand embarrassment, and sometimes people need that to escape their own reality. It also helps that this show has an endless parade of famous cameos to ensure the formula rarely feels repetitive.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Game of Thrones House Do You Belong To?
Stark · Lannister · Targaryen · Tyrell

Your drink, your weapon, your seat at the table, what you do to somebody who wrongs you. Eight quick calls and we will tell you whose banner you should actually be standing under. Four houses are still in this: the cold one, the rich one, the one with the dragons, and the one that has never needed a sword to get its way.

🐺Stark(Game of Thrones)

🦁Lannister(Game of Thrones)

🐉Targaryen(House of the Dragon)

🌹Tyrell(Game of Thrones)

CLAIM YOUR HOUSE →

01

What is your go-to at the feast?
Everybody has one, and everybody's says something.

ADark ale by the fire, nothing fancy.
BWhatever costs the most in the cellar.
CWhatever gets poured, drunk far too fast.
DOne cup, slowly, while I watch the room.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Pick a weapon off the wall.
You get one. Choose quickly.

AA greatsword, heavy and honest.
BA dagger, plus a second one nobody knows about.
CFire, obviously.
DNothing sharper than the things I can say.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Where do you end up sitting?
The seating plan is the politics.

AHigh table, quietly wishing I was outside.
BNext to whoever actually matters.
CWherever I like, because people move.
DA corner seat with a view of everyone.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

What do people get wrong about you?
Reputation arrives about a week before you do.

AThat I am cold, when I am only quiet.
BThat I say what I mean the first time.
CThat I might be bluffing.
DThat I am harmless.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

One free evening in King's Landing. Where do you go?
Nobody plots every single night.

AOut of the city entirely, heading home.
BSomewhere expensive, with people who owe me.
CWherever it is loud and slightly dangerous.
DA long dinner where everybody talks too much.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Somebody wrongs you. What happens next?
This is the real personality test in Westeros.

AI say it to their face, once.
BI wait, because they will need me eventually.
CEverybody hears about it before morning.
DThey never find out it was me.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Your people are in trouble. What is your first move?
No time to think about this one.

AI turn up, even when it is a terrible idea.
BI pay for the problem to go away.
CI go after whoever caused it.
DI already called in that favour last week.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Be honest. What do you actually want?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your house.

ATo go home, and then to stay there.
BTo own the room without sitting at the head of it.
CThe crown, with everybody watching.
DTo be the one everybody genuinely likes.

REVEAL MY HOUSE →

The Banner Is Raised
Your House Is…

Four houses, four completely different theories about how you survive a
world like this one. Here is where your banner belongs, what the name would cost you, and what it
would buy.

Game of Thrones · HBO · 2011 to 2019

House Stark

You belong in the North, where the weather does most of the
arguing and nobody is impressed by a title. The Starks are the only great house on this list
who genuinely believe that being right matters more than winning, which is exactly why the
show spent eight years punishing them for it.

Your loyalty runs to people rather than to crowns, and you would rather lose a war
honestly than win one by doing something you would have to hide.

The Stark tragedy is a simple one, since a family raised to keep its word ended up
surrounded by people who treat a promise as an opening bid.

You are the one who thinks about the winter while everybody else is still enjoying the
summer, and the realm never thanks anybody for that.

What saves the Starks in the end is not swords. It is the fact that the children grew up
and became four completely different kinds of dangerous.

Game of Thrones · HBO · 2011 to 2019

House Lannister

You belong to the house that worked out early on that gold moves
faster than armies. Casterly Rock runs on leverage, reputation and the certainty that
everybody at the table owes you something, and you are perfectly comfortable with all three.

You play a longer game than the people around you, and you would rather own the outcome
quietly than be seen winning in public.

Family is the thing you would burn the realm for, which is both the best and the very
worst quality this house has.

Tyrion, Jaime and Cersei are three of the most compelling characters on television
precisely because they were raised with everything except the ability to be simple about
it.

You are not the villain of your own story. You are simply the one who read the rules
properly and decided to use them.

House of the Dragon · HBO · Since 2022

House Targaryen

You belong to the house that conquered a continent and never
quite got over it. Targaryens do not ask for a seat at the table, because in their version
of events the table was theirs to begin with, and that certainty is either magnificent or
catastrophic depending on the week.

You feel things at full volume, and nobody who has ever met a Targaryen has described
one as measured.

House of the Dragon made the family far more interesting than the original show could,
because here the enemy is not some other house. It is the rest of the bloodline.

Season 3 landed on HBO in June 2026 and pushed the civil war into the part everybody who
read the book has been dreading for years.

Your great strength and your great problem are the same thing, which is that you
genuinely believe the story was always going to end with you.

Game of Thrones · HBO · 2011 to 2019

House Tyrell

You belong to Highgarden, where nobody raises their voice and
everybody gets exactly what they came for. The Tyrells feed the realm, charm the realm and
quietly steer the realm, and they have never once needed to win a battle to get their way.

You understand that being liked is a weapon, and you are genuinely better at it than the
people who spend their lives trying to be feared.

Olenna is the most quietly ruthless character in the entire series, and she does all of
it from a chair with a bowl of fruit in front of her.

Your house wins by being useful, since a kingdom that cannot eat without you will
forgive you almost anything.

The risk of being a Tyrell is simple enough. Charm works beautifully on everybody except
the one person who has stopped caring what anyone thinks.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

4
'Sex and the City' (1998–2004)

Image via HBO

Four best friends—columnist Carrie Bradshaw (Sarah Jessica Parker), publicist Samantha Jones (Kim Cattrall), lawyer Miranda Hobbes (Cynthia Nixon), and gallery owner Charlotte York (Kristin Davis)—navigate the highs and lows of dating, friendships, careers, and sex in the bustling world of New York City.

It's universally agreed upon that Sex and the City's fun comes from the chemistry between its leads and the sheer variety of disasters they find themselves in. Yes, Carrie may be the protagonist, but Samantha's blunt confidence, Miranda's cynicism, and Charlotte's romantic idealism are what gives the group four very different perspectives on life. Add in the fashion, glamorous New York locations, outrageous one-liners, and sheer openness of conversations, and Sex and the City remains an endlessly iconic show about sisterhood as much as it is a romantic tale.

3
'The Righteous Gemstones' (2019–2025)

Image via HBO

The Gemstone family is a wealthy and wildly dysfunctional evangelical dynasty led by televangelist Eli Gemstone (John Goodman). But just as the family attempts to expand their empire, various scandals, rivalries, criminals, and schemes threaten to tear the Gemstones apart—especially as Eli's spoiled adult children bask in their lavish lifestyles and desires.

Few HBO comedies commit to a joke as completely as The Righteous Gemstones, with every character leaning right into the gloriously obnoxious arrogance of the titular family. Better still, the show has somehow mastered the act of escalation as a petty argument can somehow lead to kidnappings, shootouts, or other criminal conspiracies. Loud, outrageous, and littered with iconic musical numbers, The Righteous Gemstones is a sensory overload. But at least underneath all the religious hypocrisy and greed lies a tale of a complicated family that genuinely loves one another.

2
'Hacks' (2021–2026)

Image via HBO

As legendary comedian Deborah Vance (Jean Smart) becomes in desperate need of a freshened-up act, she's paired up with young comedy writer Ava Daniels (Hannah Einbinder), whose career has stalled after a controversial tweet. The two initially have almost nothing in common, but their professional relationship gradually develops into a complicated friendship as they push, frustrate, and occasionally sabotage one another.

There's no better core to a comedy than a story of two wildly different personalities slowly realizing that they might actually need each other. Of course, this is perfectly executed thanks to Smart and Einbinder's chemistry, whose constant bickering becomes ridiculously entertaining—especially when it's balanced by pure moments of vulnerability. Laced with ruthless one-liners and hilarious cameos, Hacks has easily become one of the best modern comedies of the last few years. It's sharp without becoming exhausting, and it really knows when to let a joke land through an awkward silence or an absurd situation.

1
'Veep' (2012–2019)

Image via HBO

As former senator Selina Meyer (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) becomes Vice President of the United States, she quickly discovers that occupying one of the most powerful positions in the country doesn't mean she actually gets to make any decisions. Surrounded by a staff of ambitious, insecure, and frequently incompetent political operatives, Selina spends her days navigating rival politicians, public scandals, diplomatic disasters, and her own increasingly desperate attempt to advance her career.

Who doesn't love a political comedy—especially when it masterfully highlights how politics is an endless parade of petty grievances, backstabbing, and deeply avoidant individuals. Louis-Dreyfus gives Selina an extraordinary combination of confidence and panic, while the rest of the supporting cast make every conversation feel like it could descend into chaos at any moment. Veep is cynical, fast, relentlessly profane, and packed with enough memorable zingers to make even the most mundane crisis hilarious. Think of this as one of HBO's most timeless shows, especially with it bizarrely starting to emulate our current reality.

Release Date

2012 - 2019-00-00

Network

HBO Max

The fight scenes are, of course, a major draw, and yet the show's willingness to bounce between gang warfare, institutional corruption, and community dysfunction is what keeps it from becoming one-note. Plus, this show is based on an original concept by Bruce Lee himself—a fact that naturally brings an irreverent energy to the project's core.

After surviving the events of The Suicide Squad, Chris Smith (John Cena)—better known as the brutal vigilante Peacemaker—is forced to join a black-ops team on the mysterious Project Butterfly. Here, he and his mismatched team of operatives must stop a mysterious alien invasion that soon becomes a threat far stranger than anything they expected.

In true James Gunn fashion, Peacemaker finds its magic by turning a ridiculous superhero into the center of a surprisingly heartfelt comedy—all without sanding away everything that makes him awful. Leaning into Peacemaker's macho posturing, bizarre musical tastes, and dysfunctional relationships is what helps create endless opportunities for comedy. In the 18th century, wealthy aristocrat Stede Bonnet (Rhys Darby) grows tired of his privileged (and very cushy) life. As a result, he abandons everything and decides to become a pirate even though he has absolutely no idea what to do. But now, after assembling an equally unconventional crew for his ship, Stede must quickly figure things out, especially as he soon crosses paths with the legendary pirate Blackbeard (Taiki Waititi).

There's no doubt that the show's greatest strength is the sheer ridiculousness of its pirate world. Waititi's Blackbeard is less a fearsome pirate than a bored celebrity in need of a new direction, while Darby's Stede approaches piracy with the enthusiasm of someone organizing a particularly ill-advised dinner party. The result is a warm, absurd comedy where swashbuckling, disastrous schemes, and surprisingly sincere conversations about identity and love can all exist in the same episode. It's universally agreed upon that Sex and the City's fun comes from the chemistry between its leads and the sheer variety of disasters they find themselves in. Yes, Carrie may be the protagonist, but Samantha's blunt confidence, Miranda's cynicism, and Charlotte's romantic idealism are what gives the group four very different perspectives on life. Add in the fashion, glamorous New York locations, outrageous one-liners, and sheer openness of conversations, and Sex and the City remains an endlessly iconic show about sisterhood as much as it is a romantic tale.

Few HBO comedies commit to a joke as completely as The Righteous Gemstones, with every character leaning right into the gloriously obnoxious arrogance of the titular family. Better still, the show has somehow mastered the act of escalation as a petty argument can somehow lead to kidnappings, shootouts, or other criminal conspiracies. There's no better core to a comedy than a story of two wildly different personalities slowly realizing that they might actually need each other. Of course, this is perfectly executed thanks to Smart and Einbinder's chemistry, whose constant bickering becomes ridiculously entertaining—especially when it's balanced by pure moments of vulnerability. items.text:
It was a shock to fans when, earlier this month, PlayStation suddenly announced on X that it would no longer be publishing Physint. Hideo Kojima, the mastermind behind the new spiritual successor to Metal Gear Solid, says he was just as confused and surprised when Sony first delivered the news to him privately back in June. He says his mind immediately went blank and he still doesn’t know why the PS5 maker dropped his game.

“So in June, SIE said they wanted to have a Zoom call. I was so busy at that time–I had just gone to New York for a Prada event and then to LA right after,” he said in a new interview with IGN. “But anyway, I came back and we had this Zoom call. They said they can no longer fund development for Physint. I was shocked and I said, ‘What did you say?’ I couldn’t quite process what they had said. I wasn’t sure because I was in shock.”

Kojima Productions employs roughly 200 people, and the veteran game developer said he immediately started thinking about all of the implications of the deal falling through, including problems with bank loans and the need to potentially lay off tons of people who had been hired to work specifically on Physint, an espionage thriller that Kojima says will be a movie as well as a game.

He continued:

Nothing could’ve prepared me for their decision to step away from the project. So I thought, ‘What am I going to do from tomorrow?’ But from my side, I love Sony. And I don’t have any bad feelings against them because I know that it’s a tough time in the game industry.

I’ve been working with them for like 30 years… Mr. Ken Kutaragi, Mr. Hirai, I was close with them. But it’s not like that recently. I realized that, okay, this is the reality. It’s the 10th anniversary of my studio. My studio might collapse, right?

Kojima was in the call with Kojima Productions president Shinji Hirano and head of talent development Aki Saito, but wouldn’t say who was there on Sony’s side and whether it was PlayStation Studios head Hermen Hulst who delivered the news to him. The three kept the news to themselves at first. Kojima even said that the first thing he did after the meeting was go back and continue working on new pieces of the concept for Physint.

“The corporate structure of SIE is different from the Jim Ryan days,” he said. “But this was a project that we were both excited about and mutually agreed on. So because of that, the shock was even bigger in June.”

While Kojima Productions eventually landed a deal to continue making the game under Xbox, Kojima says he still doesn’t know why Sony made the sudden decision to abandon the project. “They haven’t contacted me ever since,” he said. “But I’m not fighting with Sony. We’re not in a dispute. But what I want to say is that we’ve been together for 30 years and we have this relationship. So if this was the conclusion, I would’ve wanted to hear it a little earlier. But that meeting in June, they just gave us the final notice.”

Bloomberg previously reported that part of the reasoning for Sony backing out of Physint had to do with it going over budget and missing deadlines. Death Stranding 2 also apparently didn’t sell as well as Sony hoped, and with the console maker backing away from PC, Physint would have to sell well only on PlayStation hardware to make up costs. A changing of the guard at Sony also reportedly played a role in the collaboration coming undone.

IGN‘s interview took place before Bloomberg’s report was published, but Kojima Productions has now responded to it in a new statement calling on people to take it with a “dose of skepticism,” and claiming that its relationship with Sony is still strong:

You may have seen a recent article that mentions Kojima Productions, speculating on the reasons for the change in publishing partners for Physint. ​

Normally, we would not comment on unsubstantiated speculation on the internet, but these aspersions around our relationship with PlayStation, the commercial performance of the Death Stranding franchise, and the broader production planning and investment for Physint, have reached beyond the studio and have touched our fans, our creative partners, and colleagues we have worked alongside with for three decades.​

None of the claims written came from any official or on-the-record source and as such we encourage you to take them with a dose of scepticism.​

Make no mistake, this was a serious situation for the studio with a range of potentially significant implications. While we recognize that the article may have caused alarm, we want to reassure you all, for the record: that the studio is in a healthy, profitable state, development for Physint continues to move forward with Xbox, and our relationship with PlayStation remains strong.​

Kojima reiterated the idea that there’s been no “divorce” with Sony in his interview. “I’ve always been a big Sony fan,” he said. “I’ve been using a Walkman. All my cameras are Sony. So I have no bad feelings towards them.”

Welcome to What’s On, our weekly roundup of notable shows. Here is what’s happening on TV from Sunday, September 20 to Saturday, September 26. All times are Eastern.

American Hostage (MGM+, Sunday, 9 p.m., series premiere) Based on the podcast of the same name, this 1970s-set true-crime thriller stars Jon Hamm as Fred Heckman, a beloved Indianapolis radio reporter who finds himself in the middle of a life-or-death crisis when hostage-taker Tony Kiritsis (Giovanni Ribisi) demands to be interviewed live on his radio program. The eight-episode story, which also stars Mireille Enos, Kristoffer Polaha, and William Jackson Harper, is just the first installment of a planned anthology exploring different real-life hostage crises in American history.


Youth (HBO and HBO Max, Sunday, 10 p.m., series premiere) Irish actress-writer Sharon Horgan (Catastrophe, Bad Sisters) continues her TV-comedy hot streak with this HBO romantic comedy. The multi-hyphenate stars as Alex, a London literary agent and 50-year-old divorcee who is navigating dating (she’s looking for “fun, lightly degrading sex”), and the existential dread of aging while caring for a pair of ailing parents (Brid Brennan and David Hargreaves) and a growing son (Aran Murphy, of Cillian stock). The cast also includes Sharlene Whyte, Rupert Friend, and Robbie Gee. Find The A.V. Club’s review on Sunday.


Line Of Fire (NBC, Monday, 10 p.m., series premiere) Peter Krause and Hope Davis lead this family-focused crime drama, which centers on the Hollingsworth clan, whose members work across various law-enforcement branches including the FBI, Secret Service, and the Department of Justice. items.text:
With the fall TV season getting underway, The A.V. Club‘s editor-in-chief Danette Chavez wants to know: What series—new or returning—are you most looking forward to?


As always, we invite you to contribute your own responses in the comments—and send in some prompts of your own! If you have a pop culture question you’d like us and fellow readers to answer, please email it to avqa@avclub.com.

East Of Eden (October 1, Netflix)


While The Grapes Of Wrath is the John Steinbeck novel that most people probably encountered in their high school literature courses, East Of Eden is, for my money, his best work. A sprawling, multi-generational tale about good, evil, and the choices we make between them, it’s one part Biblical allegory and one part devastating exploration of the human condition. (Seriously, if you have never read it, please fix your life.) Do I think that a seven-part Netflix adaptation can successfully contain all those multitudes? I’m not sure, but I’m intrigued enough to find out. Particularly since it stars Florence Pugh and will clearly focus heavily on Cathy Ames, infamous antiheroine and the subject of endless debate among readers and literary critics about the nature of evil. To steal an idea from Steinbeck himself: It doesn’t have to be perfect; it just has to be good. [Lacy Baugher Milas]

Carrie (October 7, Prime Video)


I’m hot and cold on Mike Flanagan. I love Hush and enjoyed his first Stephen King adaptation, Gerald’s Game. Even Dr. Sleep and Ouija: Origin Of Evil punch well above their weight. Still, the hardlines, pastel covers, and whispered performances of Hill House lost me. I skipped his Netflix era along with The Life Of Chuck, because “From the hearts and minds of Stephen King and Mike Flanagan” is a tagline that causes me to die of cringe. Chuck notwithstanding, I tend to enjoy Flanagan’s King adaptations, so his Carrie show has my attention. That’s a story that feels incredibly salient for the social media age, when teen humiliation can be live-streamed for all the world to see. Sure, an eight-episode limited series is a long time to wait for a predetermined promposal. But maybe it’ll make the pig’s blood taste all the sweeter. [Matt Schimkowitz]

Cupertino (October 8, CBS)


We’re all understandably sick of seeing real and fictional tech billionaires and AI advocates champion their nefarious agendas, so I’m most curious to see how Cupertino positions itself in this sphere. I loved co-creators Robert and Michelle King’s most recent series, Evil, and they’re clearly good at making legal dramas work, as seen with The Good Wife universe. So I have faith in them to make, at the very least, an amusing broadcast drama that I can get hooked on again. Cupertino centers on two recently fired attorneys (played by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller) who start their own firm, mainly taking on clients aiming to fight back against the Goliaths controlling Silicon Valley. I’m intrigued by both the concept and the ensemble, which includes Nik Dodani, Busy Phillips, Renée Elise Goldsberry, and Ella Stiller. [Saloni Gajjar]

The Lowdown season two (October 14, FX)


The pleasures of The Lowdown are as straightforward as they are abundant: Great premise (amiable dramedy in the vein of Lodge 49 and Terriers that chooses the journey over the destination), great cast (Ethan Hawke, Keith David, Kaniehtiio Horn, and

Ryan Kiera Armstrong are back for season two, and are joined by Betty Gilpin and Tommy Lee Jones), and a setting that grows richer by the episode (Tulsa, OK). Even if series creator Sterlin Harjo hadn’t set up another uniquely compelling mystery in the upcoming season, I’d tune in to see Hawke as Lee Raybon, a character that lets the actor continue to show off his limitless range while also being of a piece with the other searching types in his repertoire. And did I mention Betty Gilpin is in the new season?? [Danette Chavez]

VisionQuest (October 14, Disney+)


As someone who liked WandaVision about 10 percent less than everybody I know—at least, once it stopped doing the fun TV pastiche stuff, and started defaulting to serving up cross-stitch material about grief—I was a little leery about next month’s Disney+ series VisionQuest. But I can’t say they didn’t get me: The show’s trailer, rolled out at D23 last month, really sold how fun the show could be, getting James Spader’s Ultron to Blacklist his way around an imaginary house while annoying the crap out of Paul Bettany’s NuVision. I’m not sold on the wider WandaVision family material the show is clearly building toward—it also turned me off of Agatha All Along—but I’m excited to at least watch the experiment play out for a few episodes, before wider franchise obligations inevitably win out. [William Hughes]

Crystal Lake (October 15, Peacock)


As an unreasonable slasher nut, I was skeptical about a prequel series centered on Friday The 13th‘s matriarch supreme, Pamela Voorhees. The first Friday essentially covers everything we need to know about the Voorhees family’s initially tragic, subsequently horrific descent into mayhem: Little Jason disappears in the lake, Pam cracks up, and horny camp counselors get iced in all sorts of inventive ways. What else did we need to know? While I’m anticipating (maybe dreading) some creative lore expansion from A24’s Peacock series, seeing Linda Cardellini decked out in Pam’s ’70s flannel and noting showrunner Brad Caleb Kane’s impressive résumé—including Lodge 49, Fringe, and It: Welcome to Derry—has me feeling cautiously optimistic about Crystal Lake. Frankly, seeing Cardellini cut loose on her victims with edged and serrated weapons is too much fun for even this wary horror hound to pass up. [Jarrod Jones]

The Fall And Rise Of Reggie Dinkins season two (November 2, NBC)


Okay, this is a little predictable, since I’m reviewing this Tracy Morgan-Daniel Radcliffe sitcom and all. But damned if I can’t wait to see how creators Robert Carlock and Daniel Means (alongside other Tina Fey sitcom factor hands like Phil Augusta, Meredith Scardino, and more) further expand the show’s fruitful comedic sandlot of fame, football and family. Morgan and Radcliffe have crafted an unexpected but hilariously lived-in odd couple energy as disgraced former NFL running back Reggie Dinkins and disgraced former indie film darling Arthur Tobin. And Erika Alexander, playing the seemingly thankless role of Reggie’s ambitious ex-wife and the only grownup in the room, is equally funny and human. The first season’s brisk 10-episode order saw the show sprint past plenty of scenarios and character dynamics the upcoming second outing can explore, and the show’s nimble handling of the hot button issue of gambling in American sports is only going to give the absurdly talented ensemble and writers more room to maneuver. [Dennis Perkins]

Black Doves season two (November 5, Netflix)


Black Doves was a perfect holiday binge with my parents: sleek, smart, twisty, and filled with charming British banter. We’d already been hooked on Slow Horses and this is that spy show’s shadier, more interpersonally tangled cousin. Erring towards Tom Clancy rather than James Bond, the middlebrow espionage has a brutal streak, which added an enjoyable edge to the otherwise comforting series of double-crosses. I’m happy to make this an annual tradition for as long as Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw want to get up to a little wetwork, and as long as they want to spar with Sarah Lancashire over who’s really in control. Add in a few new guest stars, another organization-spanning caper, and, as the British say, I’m sat. [Jacob Oller]

Yellowjackets season four (November 20, Showtime)


With all due respect to The Gilded Age (which returns on November 1), there is no premiere this season that matches my enthusiasm for the return of Yellowjackets. This is not because I have lofty expectations of this season, but because season three was so nuts that I have been waiting for 18 months just to see how the hell they’re going to wrap it up. And while I did enjoy season three largely for its camp factor (compared to its first season, which was more successful as a straightforward thriller), the fact that Yellowjackets‘ fourth and final season sees the girls return to their high school in New Jersey should help to avoid some of the wheel-spinning that befell the show’s last outing. Given that the creator Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson already said they planned to pick up the pace this time around, I’m looking forward to seeing something crazy. [Drew Gillis]

Dig (November 23, Peacock)


Digging! Everybody’s trying it this fall, whether it’s Tom Cruise doing Kirkland Signature Dr. Strangelove in Digger, or the Parks And Recreation duo of Amy Poehler and Michael Schur in their new Peacock comedy about archaeologists who stumble upon a potentially earthshattering secret while sifting through the ruins of ancient Greece. I know nothing of the source material—the novel Excavations by real-life archaeologist Kate Myers—but I have immense faith in the creative team here, which includes Schur’s wife, Single Parents co-creator and New Girl veteran J.J. Philbin. I’ve been eager to see Geraldine Viswanathan (who’s onboard as one of Poehler’s fellow archaeologists here) back on a TV comedy, and could Hugh Laurie be any better suited for a role than that of the hidebound professor leading the titular dig, someone I’m sure will have a totally measured and not at all explosive reaction to whatever artifact of inciting incident that his colleagues pull out of the ground? Here’s hoping they dredge up a trove of laughs along with it—if not, there’s always two seasons of Digman! to fall back on. [Erik Adams]


Dig (Image: Peacock)

items.title: Single player games might require age verification if they use Steam under EU Kids Act's current draft, according to MEP's senior policy adviser
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The
items.text:
The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The draft legislation is called the EU Kids Act and calls for the setting up of a tiered system governing the types of accounts children under 15 can create to access such services, enforced by mandatory age verification for all users.

The documents laying out the proposal have been officially released, and based on the current wording the Commission have used to define what they class as an online game, it seems single player games that rely on online platforms like Steam for updates, distribution, or even a one-time authentication could be caught in the crossfire. That is, unless the definition is tightened up before the law is set in stone, if it indeed it makes it that far.

When the proposal originally leaked, prior to its official unveiling by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, reports suggested there was no detail as to how the body had defined the concept of "online games" - and by extension, which sorts of games would fall under the proposed regulations. Now it looks as if that definition is rather broad, as it stands.

For instance, in a press conference held by the Stop Killing Games campaign about the proposed act, European Pirate Party senior policy adviser Paul Diegel - who serves as an assistant to sitting European Parliament member Markéta Gregorová - noted that the current draft of the legislation would even see single player games affected "because they're connected to Steam for updates". Since the proposal docs are publicly available via the European Commission's site, I've dug out the current version of the section on what is or isn't an online game as far as the proposed act is concerned. It reads as follows:

Video games have become an important part of the digital environment in which minors participate and interact with others, in a playful, goal-oriented or entertaining manner. Certain video gaming platforms allow the dissemination and exchange of user-generated content to an indeterminate number of recipients of the service and the facilitation of contact between these recipients. Such online games fall within the definition of online platforms referred to in Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 and should be covered by the scope of this Regulation.

At the same time, some online games that do not allow the dissemination of information to an indeterminate number of recipients should also fall within the scope of this Regulation. This is the case of any game that can be played on a computer, a mobile device, or a games console, irrespective of whether the game underlying software is subsequently executed locally, remotely, such as by means of durable medium, and irrespective of whether the service is provided free of charge, against payment, or against hybrid remuneration involving in-service (or in-application) purchases.

Online games that are accessible or purchasable exclusively through physical media, without any online component enabling their access, distribution, or purchase, are not considered online games for the purposes of this Regulation. For the avoidance of doubt, where an online game also has certain features corresponding to a video sharing platform, it shall be considered an online game for the purpose of this Regulation.

If I'm reading that right, the sole exception in the current proposal applies to games that can only be bought or accessed physically, not via an online storefront like Steam. Even if the online element's only being used to distribute the game and subsequently ship updates to it, it seems like it would fall under the purview of the regulation as it's written at this stage, meaning it'd be subject to age verification.

It's worth noting that the EU Kids Act is still just a proposal at the moment. Tightening up or refining definitions such as this one, so that the law only affects exactly the sorts of games it intends to, is something I'd peg as almost certain to happen as the pending legislation is revised and scrutinised as part of the EU's lawmaking process. That means that if the Act does eventually end up being set into law, it could have a definition that only singles out specific types of online game that mirror social media, in the sense of connecting children to endless other players they can chat with or see the user-created content of.

For now, I'm gonna go and spend what remains of my Friday afternoon writing about a topic less heavy on legal jargon.

When the proposal originally leaked, prior to its official unveiling by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, reports suggested there was no detail as to how the body had defined the concept of "online games" - and by extension, which sorts of games would fall under the proposed regulations. Now it looks as if that definition is rather broad, as it stands.

For instance, in a press conference held by the Stop Killing Games campaign about the proposed act, European Pirate Party senior policy adviser Paul Diegel - who serves as an assistant to sitting European Parliament member Markéta Gregorová - noted that the current draft of the legislation would even see single player games affected "because they're connected to Steam for updates". Since the proposal docs are publicly available via the European Commission's site, I've dug out the current version of the section on what is or isn't an online game as far as the proposed act is concerned. It reads as follows:

Video games have become an important part of the digital environment in which minors participate and interact with others, in a playful, goal-oriented or entertaining manner. Certain video gaming platforms allow the dissemination and exchange of user-generated content to an indeterminate number of recipients of the service and the facilitation of contact between these recipients. At the same time, some online games that do not allow the dissemination of information to an indeterminate number of recipients should also fall within the scope of this Regulation. For the avoidance of doubt, where an online game also has certain features corresponding to a video sharing platform, it shall be considered an online game for the purpose of this Regulation.

If I'm reading that right, the sole exception in the current proposal applies to games that can only be bought or accessed physically, not via an online storefront like Steam. Even if the online element's only being used to distribute the game and subsequently ship updates to it, it seems like it would fall under the purview of the regulation as it's written at this stage, meaning it'd be subject to age verification.

That means that if the Act does eventually end up being set into law, it could have a definition that only singles out specific types of online game that mirror social media, in the sense of connecting children to endless other players they can chat with or see the user-created content of.
For now, I'm gonna go and spend what remains of my Friday afternoon writing about a topic less heavy on legal jargon.

items.title: Control Resonant review: A superbly strange action-RPG that'll make you feel tiny and godly at once
items.author: James Archer
items.summary:
Control Resonant's roaring melee battles and grasp of cosmic weirdness put this unlikely sequel up there with Remedy’s finest work.

Developer: Remedy
items.text:
Control Resonant's roaring melee battles and grasp of cosmic weirdness put this unlikely sequel up there with Remedy’s finest work.

Developer: Remedy Entertainment

Publishers: Remedy Entertainment

Release: September 24th 2026

On: Windows

From: Steam, Epic Games Store

Price: $60 / £50 / €60

Reviewed on: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 32GB RAM, Nvidia RTX 5080, Windows 11

Control Resonant review

Control Resonant, much like the inside-out, interdimensional cryptids it has you bashing with a shapeshifting stick, probably shouldn’t exist. At least not in the risk-averse, pennypinching reality that sometimes seems to have enveloped the art of gamesmaking, and that may have installed some scepticism into my own head. The sequel to a liked yet slow-selling shooter, which replaces both the original’s player character and its instantly recognisable, bureauca-brutalist setting, while violently pirouetting into open-world RPG melee brawling. Five words that Remedy, in all their thirty years of existence, have never previously let pass their lips.

But exist it does, which is fortunate, because the gamble pays off spectacularly. Resonant’s reality-bending trip across a kaleidoscopic Manhattan is as rich in stark views, eerie atmosphere, and creative quests as Control’s Oldest House ever was, driven along by strong character-first storytelling and Remedy’s best action in ages.

There is a lot of that action, so it seems like a good place to start. Control Resonant makes big changes on both sides of its fights, starting with the fact you are now Dylan Faden, brother and formerly brainwashed foe to Control’s Jesse. A sort-of free man for the first time in decades, Dylan takes to heroics with a weary but honest determination, fueled by the combined guilt over his prior bodypuppet misdeeds and concern for his now-missing sibling. Who, at least, grants him a parting gift of the Aberrant, which looks like it came from the same transforming amarments factory as Jesse's Service Weapon - just for swinging rather than shooting. Meanwhile, the people-warping Hiss and Mold are back as the main opponents, but in a positive departure, the enemy line-up is heavier on properly twisted, otherworldly foes than simple humanoids. Think floating, fuzzy megaspores, towering armless lumps with spikes for faces, and on several occasions, possessed buses. Mamdani’s New York, eh.

Mathematically, combat starts simple. Each Aberrant form - i.e., your weapons - gets its own button and a three-hit combo. Primary and secondary forms have three choices each, a kind of Whacking Things Greatest Hits of hammers, scythes, and nunchuks, plus your pick of a distinct combo finisher.

Pick up the cadence of these one-against-all battles, though – and factor in the active combat abilities you earn through boss victories – and Resonant’s melee starts clicking. And expanding. And exploding. Encounters are relentless, a barrage of enemy attacks matched only by Dylan’s own supernatural damage dealing, both parties busting their moves in storms of sparks, debris, and extradimensional haze. Aberrant hits and power deployments flow into each other beautifully, and even without engaging the manual lock-on, the game is uncannily good at interpreting which foe you’re trying to strike, so there’s little cause for frustration as you rapidly flick between opponents.

After a few upgrades, it’s possible to craft reliable stance break builds, particularly through combinations of the status effects that certain abilities specialise in. This can then turn Resonant’s already-satisfying slugging matches into something that resembles Doom Eternal as much as Devil May Cry, Dylan whooshing around arenas to chain together executions (themselves as gratifyingly animated as Doom’s) and snowball off their strength, healing, and poise damage buffs.

I still think the original Control’s combat is better than it’s sometimes described, especially if you invest in furniture-throwing, but it simply isn’t as dynamic or aggressive as this. Parrying? Never heard of it – Dylan has a dodge, but the skill tree tunes even that to serve as a proactive attack-boosting tool, rather than just a means of avoiding harm. Resonant wants its players to push. Begs for it, practically, and nearly thirty hours in, I’m still happy to oblige.

Difficulty-wise, Control Resonant is no Sekiro, though it can get tricky in its larger-scale fights (or if you neglect to keep the Aberrant fed with upgrades). However, it also has an impressively granular Assists menu, where you can customise individual combat aspects, down to minutiae like enemy projectile speed and perfect dodge window length. Some of these adjust both ways too, so you can crank up the challenge if desired.

The only places where Remedy’s character action inexperience peeps through are the boss battles. Some genuinely are enjoyable, one-on-one paranatural duels, though others are overly simple, their sense of threat owed to massive health bars and the sheer damage of their attacks – not the challenge of recognising and avoiding them. They do all have the striking and memorable visual design you’d want from an action-RPG boss, at least, and their reward of potentially build-altering new combat powers meant I never felt I was wasting my time going after them.

Resonant is also smart in how it handles upgrades and levelling up more generally. Spending points and materials on a single Aberrant form will buff the base damage and falter build-up for all forms, so while resources are scarce enough that you’ll still need to make decisions on which to prioritise – I, for one, fell in love with the clanking, stunlocking, poise-evaporating power of the secondary Drill form – you’re still incentivised to spend leftovers on less favoured weapons. This, simultaneously, keeps them at least fairly viable later in the game, so power doesn’t come at the cost of flexibility.

Dylan’s own talent tree also has, unusually, a geographical element. Beating enemies and completing side missions in one of Manhattan’s various sub-areas will essentially level up the area itself, improving drop rates, healing item potency, and the stock of the local resource vendor. It’s only with each new area level that Dylan himself gets a skill point to put into his tree (which, for the record, is bigger than chuffin' Yggdrasil). Defeating that region’s boss also 'resets' the area, respawning and toughening up roaming enemies in exchange for a fresh set of XP-bountiful side activities.

It’s a peculiar mechanism, but again, one that works. Tying power progression to time and effort spent in different areas motivates exploration, arguably more so than simply slathering the map in question marks, and in my mind created a tidy, almost Elden Ring-like loop of 'Get rewards, challenge boss, get rewards.' Lending, in turn, a more tangible and digestible structure to the open world.

That’s an open world, by the way, that absolutely stands up as a successor to the Oldest House. Not that some concrete-walled cameos are any less welcome, but Resonant manages to spread the original’s New Weirdness wider without it getting thinner. There are still loads of flavoursome oddities painted into the city’s details: redacted files dropped by fleeing agents, billboards making less sense as the patterning around them worsens, disturbed objects falling in the ‘correct’ direction as Dylan uses gravity anomalies to walk on ceilings and walls – meaning a messy, inverted fight can send pallets of detritus shooting up into the air. Best of all are the sidequests, which tend to focus on the imaginatively bizarre Altered Items that have escaped the House’s containment cells. Calming a stressed lightbulb, or singing to a room of terrified dancers in ritualistic karaoke, can be both funny and a pleasant cooldown from the tautness of the combat.

It’s never wacky, mind. Resonant’s strangeness is just as often played for drama, and quite successfully, in terms of how often it makes Dylan – and perhaps all of humanity – feel like some kind of cosmic sand grain. Expeditions into massive, impossible spaces; a soundtrack that knows when to hype and when to haunt; lingering mysteries around the invading forces; they all conspire to stoke a lonely, forlorn chill. A fear, really, of the unknowable, and of how for all Dylan’s superhuman strength, he’s still just one bloke with a metal bar and bad memories of life as his employers’ teenage lab rat. Which is cool! Sometimes being reminded of how small you are is necessarily to reinforce the story’s extinction-level stakes, before you can whip out that scythe again and rage against the dying of the light.

It bears noting that amid this raging, Resonant remains focused on itself, which is to say it goes light on the Remedyverse crossover stuff. I haven’t checked off every sidequest yet but at least in the main story, there’s no fanfare moment where the outline of Alan Wake ghosts into view, no big Old Gods of Asgard musical number, etcetera. Which, given how shrewdly the overlaps were worked into Control, Alan Wake II, and especially the latter’s The Lake House DLC, is a minor shame. There is, at least, one tune-heavy sequence that plays like a calmer, nonviolent Ashtray Maze tribute, plus a liberal sprinkling of lyrical tracks elsewhere, so the series' banger credentials stay intact for now.

Instead, the story puts a redemption-seeking Dylan front and centre, anchored by relationships with the two women in his life. Jesse, who’s off on a mission of her own, co-stars in a series of interestingly novel flashback sequences, leaving handler Zoe as the more regular presence. Zoe communicates mainly in Firewatch-esque radio dialogue to which you pick responses on the fly, choosing to show anger, reservedness, or the Dylan Special: guilt. This is not a branching kind of RPG, but this extra dash of agency is a nice way of better aligning with your character’s thoughts and reactions than was true of the original Control. And the regularity of Zoe’s chats – which you can often instigate yourself – makes sure they stay effective, convincing building blocks for a blossoming friendship that may not otherwise have felt earned.

On the technical side, Resonant also looks the business, Remedy’s love for ray/path tracing and some of the less problematic DLSS tech being even more apparent here than in Alan Wake II. Its supposed Steam Deck support hasn’t quite panned out, however, with potato settings and heavy FSR upscaling failing to keep it above 30fps in busy city scenes. In truth, the whole thing could use another polish patch as well, as I’ve had a few instances of background music briefly cutting out, or enemies getting stuck on scenery. On one occasion I was slapped through a wall after biffing a dodge, which ironically progressed me slightly further through the mission, though less helpful was the bug that kept resetting my outfit choices when loading or fast-travelling to a certain region in the postgame.

I can forgive a few scuff marks, though, when they're acquired in the process of bold thinking and radical redesigning on this scale. That Remedy have realised this ambition with such rousing action, and a truly fresh take on one of the most well-trodden locales in games, is worthy of applause. Hopefully that this isn’t the last we see of the Faden twins, even if the next one is a cel-shaded fishing sim or something.

items.title: Dog in the Machine reinvents the domino tactics of Into The Breach as a mecha dog show, with players teaching their hounds tricks
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: If the organisers of Crufts ever have to produce a season of Robot Wars, the results probably won't be a million miles away from Dog in the Machine - a new
items.text:
If the organisers of Crufts ever have to produce a season of Robot Wars, the results probably won't be a million miles away from Dog in the Machine - a new turn-based tactics puzzler that's sort of Into The Breach but with a greater emphasis on props and tricks.

The story in brief: it's Future-O-Clock, and we humans all live in a whirring mecha-city, attended by our loyal mecha-dogs (it's not clear to me what's happened to actual, flesh-and-blood dogs - hopefully we haven't rendered them extinct through in-breeding, or slaughtered them to make lard). Except that oh blast, humans have just been exiled from the city, due to causes unknown.

In our absence, the city's infurnal cleaning bots are trying to break down all of our beloved labrobodoodles for parts. How pawful! Fortunately, the handsome electrohounds absolutely excel at teeing up domino-chain reactions on modestly sized grid maps. Here's a trailer.

Watch on YouTube

Developers Studio Chahut and publishers Goblinz Publishing have just reminded me that Dog in the Machine has a release date - 27th September. Thanks to that email, I became aware of Dog in the Machine's demo, which I have now played a little and enjoyed. In each level, you move your Autodog around to defeat a bunch of bots. You've got a limited energy supply to bestow on regular moves and repeatable "core" attacks, once-per-turn special abilities, and wildcard "tricks" such as duplicating the previous special ability, or "teleporting" by way of a tunnel.

Given that you're outnumbered, you've got to be efficient and preferably, turn enemies against each other. A simple strategy is using a charging bite to knock one foe into the path of another's attack. A more complex approach is to exploit terrain fixtures such as conveyor belts or impact-triggered laser defences. Very Into The Breachy, yes, though it's relatively relaxed, as you can undo moves without penalty, and it feels like there's a greater focus on the terrain fixtures. Some of the maps are like pinball machines, almost.

In addition to trashing the rampaging roombas, you've got to worry about an alarm bar gauge that ends the game once filled. Enemies add points to it, but you can remove those points by damaging and destroying them. It's a bit like the alert system in Invincible Inc, though it doesn't seem as elaborate.

I like the cartoon sci-fi aesthetics. It's all very colourful, clicky-clacky and burbly-whirry. I also like the idea that the whole thing is sort of an agility competition in disguise. So far, the "tricks" are just familiar gambits like boosting your attack stat for a turn, but I hold out hope that Studio Chahut have based a few on, say, pole weaving or playing fetch.

The only thing I really don't like is the title. It's a reference to "ghost in the machine", Gilbert Ryle's best-known line critiquing Cartesian dualism. If they'd gone with Dog Ex Machina, referencing "deus ex machina" from theatre, they could have done a joke about "dog" being "god" spelled backwards, and duped innocent Steam users into thinking that it's an Ion Storm revival, for good measure. See, this is why I should exit games journalism and become a highly paid consultant. Read more and try the demo for yourself on Steam.

Update: ...or maybe Dog in the Machine is actually a riff on "cog in the machine". Thanks Reflector. I withdraw my proposal to become a highly paid consultant.
